question: In all of the following enzyme deficiencies, hyperammonemia is a common feature, EXCEPT:
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: "Argininosuccinate synthetase deficiency" -> "impaired conversion of citrulline and aspartate to argininosuccinate" -> "increased ammonia due to inability to detoxify" -> 95%
CHAIN: "Carbamoyl Phosphate synthetase (CPS-I) deficiency" -> "reduced urea cycle function" -> "accumulation of ammonia in the bloodstream" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC) deficiency" -> "disruption of the urea cycle" -> "hyperammonemia due to ammonia accumulation" -> 90%
CHAIN: "Ornithine amino transferase deficiency" -> "possible alternative metabolic pathway" -> "less direct impact on ammonia levels" -> "unclear if hyperammonemia is common" -> 70%
analysis: The question asks which enzyme deficiency does not commonly lead to hyperammonemia. The urea cycle is crucial for detoxifying ammonia, and deficiencies in certain enzymes can lead to increased ammonia levels. Argininosuccinate synthetase, Carbamoyl Phosphate synthetase (CPS-I), and Ornithine transcarbamoylase (OTC) deficiencies are all known to cause hyperammonemia due to their roles in the urea cycle. In contrast, ornithine amino transferase (also known as ornithine transaminase) deficiency primarily affects the conversion of ornithine to citrulline and does not have a direct impact on ammonia levels, making it the exception among the listed options. Therefore, the most likely correct answer is 'Ornithine amino transferase.'
